item.title: It is not that storms bypass China, but that we have built a steady shield: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
It is not that storms bypass China, but that we have built a steady shield: Global Times editorial This autumn of 2026 lays bare a stark contrast between a turbulent world and China's stable governance. On one side, the ongoing conflict in the Middle East keeps roiling global energy supplies. Diesel prices in Europe and the US have climbed to an all time high of around $220 per barrel. Meanwhile, France and wider Europe are gripped by sustained unrest, with long simmering social contradictions boiling over. On the other side, China presents a vastly different picture over the same period. Nationwide cross regional trips reached 2.144 billion over the seven day National Day holiday, bringing the combined figure for the Mid Autumn and National Day holidays close to 2.8 billion as people traveled across the country. In September, China's consumer price index (CPI) rose by just 0.9 percent year on year, while food prices actually fell by 1.7 percent. The world is in turmoil, yet ordinary Chinese people can still plan trips and live their lives with peace of mind. Many are asking why the global crises unfolding elsewhere seem to have limited impact on China. The answer is straightforward: It's not that the storm has automatically veered off course; it's that we have preemptively shielded people's livelihoods from these risks. Ample, diversified stockpiles form the first "flood retention zone" that stabilizes prices, preventing violent swings in international markets from spilling over into households' grocery baskets and store shelves. As the world's largest crude oil importer, China's crude imports tumbled to roughly 8.1 million barrels per day in the second quarter. Imports fell below 8 million barrels per day in May and June, hitting the lowest level since 2016. Even so, there was no shortage of refined oil supply domestically. Industry estimates that China's strategic petroleum reserves are ample. Together with substantial inventories of refined products, these reserves provide a reliable buffer at the onset of a crisis. Where others face immediate supply collapse once shipments are cut off, China holds sufficient reserves to stay calm. At the same time, the bottom line of China's food security remains firmly secured. Summer grain output in 2026 surpassed 300 billion jin (150 million tonnes) for the first time. The country's daily capacity to process and supply grain and edible oils exceeds 1.8 million tons for each category. These national stockpiles grant China ample room for maneuver amid external shocks. A complete and highly resilient industrial chain acts as a "wave breaking dyke" that dampens the transmission of risks. Shocks from rising global commodity prices are absorbed and softened at successive links along the industrial chain, so their impact on end consumer goods is greatly diluted by the time they reach shoppers. To be clear, China is not immune to external shocks - as reflected in that 32 percent quarter on quarter drop in crude imports in Q2. But production never ground to a halt. In September, the value added output of industrial enterprises above designated size rose 5.5 percent year on year, with a 5.3 percent cumulative gain for the first three quarters. Manufacturing output grew 6.0 percent, automobile manufacturing by 6.7 percent, and electronics manufacturing surged by 16.4 percent. While fierce storms rage abroad, our factories keep running and industrial links hold firm. That is our source of confidence. Behind this lies the resilience provided by China's diversified energy system. In the first nine months of this year, domestic output of raw coal from industrial enterprises above designated size reached 3.45 billion tons, crude oil 164.6 million tons, and natural gas 196.7 billion cubic meters. In September, nuclear, wind and solar power generation increased by 21.5 percent, 10.6 percent and 19.5 percent year-on-year, respectively. By the end of August, installed photovoltaic capacity surpassed that of coal-fired power for the first time in history, becoming China's largest source of installed power generation capacity. When the price of one energy source rises, alternative sources can quickly step in to fill the gap. More importantly, China's industrial chains have mechanisms for absorbing and sharing costs, meaning that rising raw material prices are not simply passed directly on to consumers. In September, national industrial producer purchase prices rose 6.9 percent year-on-year, while prices in upstream coal mining surged 35.3 percent and those in oil and gas extraction climbed 24.5 percent year-on-year. By proactively reducing profit margins and flexibly adjusting production schedules, the domestic refining and petrochemical sector, in conjunction with the refined oil price regulation mechanism, ultimately limited the year-over-year increase in domestic retail prices for refined oil products to 16.6 percent. In some other countries, the surge in global oil prices has translated directly into higher household expenses. Why is China consistently able to build a solid bulwark against turbulent winds and rough seas? The answer lies in an efficient, well-coordinated and proactive government that takes a holistic approach and intervenes when necessary to provide timely support. Ahead of the summer peak in energy demand, the government made early arrangements to ensure energy supplies nationwide. A high proportion of medium- and long-term contracts for thermal coal, electricity and natural gas were signed and fulfilled, laying a solid foundation for stable supplies and prices. This summer, China's national peak electricity demand set new records three times, reaching a high of 1.553 billion kilowatts. Yet coal inventories at centrally dispatched power plants consistently remained sufficient for more than 30 days of consumption. Not a single province experienced power rationing, and no region had to implement rolling blackout. Faced with a massive travel surge totaling 2.144 billion passenger trips during China's National Day holiday, public security, transportation and meteorological authorities worked in coordination to support road travel, with self-driving trips accounting for more than 90 percent of journeys. Travel by new-energy vehicles reached 1.8 times the usual daily level, while expressways continued to operate smoothly even as traffic peaked at 71 million vehicles on the first day of the holidays. It is precisely the combination of an efficient market and a proactive government that ensures economic and social activities can be effectively organized and coordinated. Looking ahead, global turbulence will not easily disappear, and new "gray rhino" and "black swan" events could emerge at any moment. China has never been sheltered from the storms sweeping the world. What makes a major country truly great is not merely its vast size or its loud voice, but its ability to ensure that, even amid raging storms, ordinary people can still buy their daily groceries, turn on the lights and begin another ordinary day with peace of mind. Those 2.144 billion passenger trips represent more than just a travel boom. They are also a confident testament to the country's chosen path of development. It is not that the storms have passed China by, but that China has kept their full force from disrupting the everyday lives of hundreds of millions of people. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. item.title: APEC ministers eye greater cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
APEC ministers eye greater cooperation From left: Eduardo Pedrosa, executive director of the APEC Secretariat; Finance Minister Lan Fo'an; and Vice Finance Minister Liao Min attend a press conference following the conclusion of the APEC Finance Ministers' Meeting in Hong Kong on Wednesday. ANDY CHONG/CHINA DAILY The latest deliverables secured at the just-concluded Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Finance Ministers' Meeting are set to provide guidance for deepening regional financial cooperation and build momentum for outcomes in the financial field at the upcoming APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, officials and experts said. After a day and a half of "candid, in-depth and constructive discussions", as Chinese Finance Minister Lan Fo'an described, the meeting in Hong Kong adopted the 2026 APEC Finance Ministers' Joint Statement and released a policy statement on digital infrastructure financing across the Asia-Pacific region. The meeting also produced two deliverables including the "Report on Supporting Households and Investing in Human Capital: Fiscal Policy Considerations for Sustaining Economic Growth in APEC" and the "Compendium on Financial Access and Opportunity for All", Lan told a news conference on Wednesday. Furthermore, member economies agreed to advance capacity building and exchanges for young financial professionals in the Asia-Pacific region, he added. As the final sectoral ministerial-level meeting ahead of the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, next month, the gathering helped "cement consensus on fiscal and financial cooperation" in response to the region's economic challenges, said Lou Feipeng, a researcher at Postal Savings Bank of China. "These outcomes have laid solid groundwork for forging consensus on fiscal and financial policies at the leaders' meeting," Lou said. According to Lan, the finance minister, the meeting also reinforced regional consensus on strengthening macroeconomic policy communication and coordination, advancing practical fiscal and financial cooperation and deepening regional integration. The meeting is important because the global economy is undergoing a lot of uncertainties, such as inflation and the rise in long-term interest rates, said Yang Jun-sok, an economics professor at the Catholic University of Korea in Seoul. To better navigate economic uncertainty and instability, all members agreed on the need to keep macroeconomic policies sound, step up policy coordination and bolster the resilience of fiscal and financial systems, said Lan, adding that APEC has shown "a greater sense of responsibility" in strengthening macroeconomic policy coordination. In a push to advance practical fiscal and financial cooperation, the policy statement on digital infrastructure financing aims to bolster regional trade, strengthen economic connectivity and expand economic opportunities for all, according to the statement. "We encourage governments to create supportive policy and regulatory conditions, and the private sector to provide capital and develop innovative financing models," said Lan, calling on multilateral development banks to help prepare projects and mobilize investment. Members also stressed the importance of financial inclusion, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises, while highlighting how fiscal support for households and investment in people can spur consumption, bolster domestic demand and lift productivity, Lan said. Highlighting the current international environment, Lan added: "These deliverables and the consensus we have reached reflect the APEC family's spirit of solidarity, inclusiveness and mutual learning." The next step is to turn deliverables and consensus into concrete action, said Lou from Postal Savings Bank of China, calling for regular macroeconomic policy dialogue to assess risks from inflation, debt and capital flows and share experience in using fiscal policy to stabilize growth. Liu Zhihua contributed to this story. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: China-U.S. friendship draws strength from youth exchanges
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
China-U.S. friendship draws strength from youth exchanges American students visiting China learn to write Chinese calligraphy at Tsinghua University. (People's Daily/Liu Lingling) "The hope of the China-U.S. relationship lies in our people, and its future lies with the young. I am glad to announce an invitation for 100,000 young Americans to visit China for exchanges and study in the coming five years." In September this year, during his state visit to the United States, Chinese President Xi Jinping announced this new initiative to promote people-to-people exchanges between the two countries. In response, a China-U.S. youth exchange event themed "Embark on a New Journey: Together We Meet, Together We Embrace the Future" was recently held in Beijing. More than 200 Chinese and American students gathered in the city for themed visits and roundtable discussions, drawing closer to one another and building lasting friendships through face-to-face interaction. During his visit to the United States in November 2023, Xi proposed inviting 50,000 young Americans to China for exchanges and study over five years, giving fresh impetus to youth exchanges between the two countries in the new era. Over the past two years and more, many Chinese and American young people have broadened their horizons and gained a better understanding of the world through exchanges and mutual learning. From classroom learning and cultural experiences to city visits and community activities, their firsthand experiences and genuine friendships have offered vivid examples of how the peoples of the two countries can come to know and appreciate one another. Having achieved the original "50,000 in five years" target two and a half years ahead of schedule, China has now launched the "100,000 in five years" initiative. The increase from 50,000 to 100,000 represents more than a numerical target. It reflects a stronger commitment and greater opportunities for young people from both countries to get to know one another, deepen mutual understanding, and grow together. During their visits, American students have walked along the Great Wall, explored the galleries of the National Museum of China, and observed breakthroughs in university research laboratories -- exposing them to a country where ancient heritage coexists with rapid modernization. Beside the battlements of the Great Wall, one student reflected that experiencing the country firsthand had dispelled many stereotypes formed across the Pacific. During roundtable discussions, young people were pleasantly surprised to discover that, despite growing up in very different environments, their peers on the other side of the ocean shared many of the same interests. Young Chinese and Americans sing the song "It's Great to Know You" at a China-U.S. exchange activity held at Peking University. (People's Daily/Liu Lingling) These face-to-face encounters and heart-to-heart conversations are sowing the seeds of understanding and trust. Little by little, they are reshaping how a new generation in China and the United States sees the other, turning distant perceptions across the Pacific into vivid, personal experiences. Exchanges extend beyond cultural experiences to discussions of frontier technologies and issues of shared concern for humanity. During roundtable discussions, Chinese and American students exchanged views freely on artificial intelligence, scientific and technological innovation, and social responsibility. Young people in both countries share the same planet and a common responsibility for the future. Faced with shared development opportunities and global challenges, they are among the most creative and action-oriented members of society. The understanding and trust built today will provide a solid foundation for cooperation tomorrow. With the "100,000 in five years" initiative as a new starting point, more young Chinese and Americans can learn from each other, make progress together and become envoys of friendship across the Pacific, helping bring their peoples closer and promote the steady and sustained development of bilateral relations. Mutual understanding and goodwill between the peoples have always been the deepest foundation and most enduring source of strength for China-U.S. relations. "Ping-Pong diplomacy" opened the door to exchanges after years of estrangement. The enduring ties forged in Kuliang have carried friendship across generations, while sub-regional cooperation has produced heartwarming stories in places such as Iowa. Countless small acts of engagement between ordinary people have come together to nourish the relationship between the two countries. Recent polls by several major U.S. polling organizations show that American public sentiment toward China has continued to improve. A survey by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs found that 57 percent of Americans polled supported "friendly cooperation and engagement with China." U.S. media outlets have also noted that short-video platforms are becoming a window through which young Americans can learn about China. People-to-people exchanges require sustained, careful efforts and long-term commitment. They help friendship between the two peoples take deeper root and grow stronger over time. This is precisely why every sincere encounter between young Chinese and Americans is so precious and deserves to be cherished. Friendships built on sincerity can last long. From "50,000 in five years" to "100,000 in five years," the friendships forged among young people in China and the United States will come together to generate powerful momentum for the sound and stable development of bilateral relations. China stands ready to continue deepening people-to-people ties and cultural exchanges with the United States, strengthen the foundation of friendship between the two peoples, and build up a lasting groundswell of public support for a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability. item.title: Chinese premier says China, Russia serve as valuable force for stability in turbulent world
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
Chinese premier says China, Russia serve as valuable force for stability in turbulent world Chinese Premier Li Qiang meets with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, Russia, Oct. 21, 2026. (Xinhua/Huang Jingwen) ST. PETERSBURG, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang said on Wednesday that against the backdrop of a continuously evolving and complex international situation, China and Russia have maintained close coordination, serving as a valuable force for stability in a world marked by turbulence and transformation. Li made the remarks when meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg. Li first conveyed cordial greetings and best wishes from Chinese President Xi Jinping to Putin, noting that since the beginning of this year, the two heads of state have met twice and made further plans for deepening China-Russia relations and cooperation. China is willing to work with Russia to strengthen strategic communication, consolidate political mutual trust, expand all-round mutually beneficial cooperation, and continuously enhance the well-being of the two peoples, he said. Li noted that China is ready to work with Russia to better leverage their economic complementarity, maintain the sound momentum of bilateral cooperation, strengthen practical cooperation in energy and resources, trade and investment, transportation and other areas, deliver more positive outcomes and promote common prosperity in both countries. The two sides should ensure the success of the China-Russia Years of Education, continuously deepen exchanges and cooperation in culture, tourism, sports and youth, and further enhance mutual understanding and friendship between the two peoples, Li said. Noting that unilateralism and hegemonism are rampant in today's world, Li said China is ready to strengthen communication and coordination with Russia on major issues, enhance coordination within multilateral platforms such as the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and BRICS, unite more forces of the Global South to safeguard common interests and uphold fairness and justice. For his part, Putin asked Li to convey his sincere greetings to Xi and wished the upcoming fifth plenary session of the 20th Central Committee of the Communist Party of China a success. Putin said that he and Xi had met several times this year and reached new important consensus on advancing the Russia-China comprehensive strategic partnership of coordination for a new era. Since the establishment of the Russia-China prime ministers' regular meeting mechanism 30 years ago, it has earnestly implemented the achievements of head-of-state diplomacy and promoted the deepening and substantive cooperation between the two sides, Putin said. Russia-China relations are built on the basis of equality and mutual respect, mutual benefit and win-win results, and accommodation of each other's concerns, he said, noting that bilateral relations are not affected by changes in the international landscape and not subject to interference from any third party. China has been and will always be Russia's closest and most reliable partner, Putin noted. Russia is ready to deepen practical cooperation with China in such areas as energy, agriculture, space, civilian nuclear energy, information technology, artificial intelligence and transportation, jointly ensure the success of the Russia-China Years of Education, and expand people-to-people and cultural exchanges, he said. Putin added that Russia supports China in hosting the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting this year and in assuming the BRICS chairmanship next year. Chinese Premier Li Qiang meets with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, Russia, Oct. 21, 2026. (Xinhua/Shen Hong) Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Xi Jinping's new Long March
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
Xi Jinping's new Long March A drone photo taken on April 16, 2026 shows students taking part in a memorial event at a monument commemorating the departure of the Central Red Army during the Long March, in Yudu County, east China's Jiangxi Province. (Xinhua/Wan Xiang) BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- On the banks of the Yudu River in east China, a choir sang of soldiers leaving home more than nine decades ago. Beside the singers, eight large red Chinese characters proclaimed: "May the spirit of the Long March shine forever." In October 1934, some 86,000 Red Army soldiers crossed the river, little knowing that they were embarking on a grueling 12,500-kilometer journey, which American journalist Edgar Snow hailed as "an odyssey unequaled in modern times." In October 1936, three main Red Army forces converged in northwestern China, marking the end of the Long March. As China commemorates the 90th anniversary of the Long March's victorious conclusion this year, visitors have traveled to the mountainous county of Yudu in Jiangxi Province to see where it all began. Yudu's visitors number in the millions each year. Among those who have made the trip is Chinese President Xi Jinping. During his visit in May 2019, Xi laid a floral basket at a Long March departure monument, went to the river crossing used by Red Army soldiers and met their descendants. "I have come here to let people across the country know that the Party has not forgotten its original aspiration," said Xi, who is also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission. "We must build on the past, pack our bags and set out again," he said. CARRY THE BATON FORWARD The Long March was a strategic shift. In 1934, the fledgling CPC was forced to abandon its main base in the provinces of Jiangxi and Fujian after failing to repel the Kuomintang regime's fifth encirclement and suppression campaign. The maneuver took the Red Army across nearly 100 rivers and more than 40 towering mountains, and through marshland known as a "death zone." The troops fought more than 600 battles. Many lost their lives along the way. Far in the northwest, Xi's father, Xi Zhongxun, and his comrades Liu Zhidan and Xie Zichang established the Shaanxi-Gansu revolutionary base. The existence of the base was an important factor in Mao Zedong's decision to make it the Long March's final destination. After the Long March, the Party established a firm foothold in northern Shaanxi, with Yan'an as its headquarters for more than a decade. From there, it grew in strength, led the Chinese people in fighting against Japanese invasion and eventually overthrew the Kuomintang regime. Growing up in such a revolutionary family, Xi developed a deep connection to the Long March and the region. He was not yet 16 when he left Beijing for a village in Yan'an, where he spent seven years living and working alongside farmers. There, he joined the Party, became the village Party chief, forged close ties with local people, and made a commitment to serving the people through public office. Yan'an, the Chinese revolution's foothold after the Long March and its springboard for national victory, was thus the starting point of Xi's political journey. "Whenever I went to Yan'an in those years, I felt a deep sense of reverence and excitement," Xi recalled. A drone photo taken on June 16, 2026 shows a view of Yan'an in northwest China's Shaanxi Province. (Xinhua/Shao Rui) As a young man, Xi was deeply fascinated by the history of the Long March. In the 1980s, he was acquainted with writer Wang Yuanjian, who devoted himself to chronicling the Red Army's heroism. Wang had interviewed many Long March veterans. As he recounted their stories, Xi would pull a notebook from his pocket and carefully take notes, Wang's wife recalled in an article. In 1996, while serving as Fujian's deputy Party secretary, Xi joined a 1,000-person torch relay marking the Long March's 60th anniversary. He set off at the front alongside an 82-year-old Red Army veteran. In 2006, as Party secretary of Zhejiang, Xi visited a photo exhibition marking the 70th anniversary of the Long March. He described the Long March as both an extraordinary test of the human spirit and will, and a journey in pursuit of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Since taking the top office in late 2012, Xi has retraced the Long March routes on visits across the country: from Yudu, where the Central Red Army assembled and set out, to Quanzhou, where soldiers fought the bloody Battle of the Xiangjiang River; Zunyi, the site of a decisive turning point; and Jiangtaibu, where Red Army forces joined up at the end of the Long March. At museums, Xi studied artifacts and asked questions. At monuments, he paid tribute to revolutionary martyrs by presenting flower baskets and bowing. He also instructed authorities to recover and properly bury soldiers' remains and build memorial facilities. On one visit, he paused before a painting of Chen Shuxiang, whose division served as the Red Army's rear guard. Captured after covering the main force's river crossing, Chen refused to surrender and died after tearing open his abdominal wound. Xi asked how the Red Army had broken through encirclement and held together despite devastating losses, then offered his answer: the power of conviction. For generations of Chinese leaders, the Long March is not just a military campaign, but a metaphor for the ongoing task of transforming China. In 1949, more than a decade after the Long March ended, the People's Republic was founded. Earlier that year, with victory in sight, Mao said that winning the revolution "would be only the first step of the Long March." The journey of building a new China had just begun. It significantly gained pace with the launch of the reform and opening up in 1978. Deng Xiaoping, a Long March veteran, proposed a three-step strategy for China's modernization, which was later elaborated as follows: meet the people's basic needs of food and clothing by 1990, achieve moderate prosperity by the end of the 20th century, and basically attain modernization by the middle of the 21st century. This modernization drive came to be known as the new Long March. "The Long March of our generation is to attain the 'two centenary goals' and realize the Chinese Dream -- the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation," Xi said. The two goals refer to achieving moderate prosperity in all respects by the Party's centenary in 2021 and building a great modern socialist country in all respects by the centenary of the People's Republic around the middle of the century. In 2017, Xi brought forward the timetable for basically achieving modernization under Deng's three-step strategy by 15 years to 2035. "Every generation must undertake its own Long March," Xi said. BRAVE THROUGH ALL ODDS When the Long March began, the Red Army faced an enemy superior in both numbers and weaponry. Kuomintang forces pursued it from behind and blocked the routes ahead, seeking to encircle and destroy it. Breaking through meant fighting for every chance of survival. In the winter of 1934, the struggle reached a critical point at the Xiangjiang River. Under heavy bombardment, Red Army troops fought their way toward the crossing points. By the time the army broke through, its ranks had dwindled from some 86,000 at the start of the march to just over 30,000. The new Long March Xi is leading would test the Party's resolve against a different set of challenges. When he was elected the Party's top leader in 2012, China had become the world's second-largest economy and largest manufacturer after more than three decades of rapid economic growth. That transformation also brought new challenges. China needed to sustain its economic momentum while narrowing regional disparities, tackling corruption, eradicating absolute poverty, and easing mounting environmental pressures. Meanwhile, the international community's expectations for China were rising. Talking about "today's Long March," Xi said that although the conditions and tasks differ greatly, it remains "a pioneering, arduous and complex undertaking." The modernization drive Xi now leads is unprecedented in human history. A population exceeding 1.4 billion is collectively advancing toward modernity on a scale surpassing the combined populations of existing developed nations. His goal is common prosperity for all, encompassing both material wealth and cultural-ethical advancement. Harmony between humanity and nature is emphasized. China also pursues rejuvenation through peaceful development. None of these is easy. Xi believes that overcoming the risks and challenges on the new journey requires the same revolutionary will forged during the Long March. "No matter how great the difficulties, think of the Red Army's Long March, and think of the bloody battle at the Xiangjiang River," he said. A humanoid robot greets people at an artificial intelligence distribution center in Nanjing, east China's Jiangsu Province, on Dec. 4, 2025. (Xinhua/Ji Chunpeng) He put forward a series of visionary strategies to ensure the march proceeds in the right direction. These include an extensive reform package -- the most comprehensive in history -- that gives the market a "decisive" role in allocating resources while making sure the government better fulfills its role. He promises broader market access for foreign investors. Since 2013, the number of pilot free trade zones in China has expanded from one to the current total of 23. He put forward a new development philosophy that places greater emphasis on innovation, coordination, green development, openness and shared benefits. All these echo the important experience drawn from the Long March -- acting on one's own initiative, seeking truth from facts, and proceeding from reality. More recently, Xi introduced "new quality productive forces" -- his term for growth driven by technological advances and industrial upgrading. Like his predecessors during the Long March, Xi leads from the front, demonstrating his strategic vision and decisiveness. Upon visiting an automobile factory years ago, he called for a shift from conventional fuel-powered vehicles to new-energy vehicles, identifying the transition as the future of China's auto industry. Over a decade ago, Xi urged China's top scientists to pay attention to a "robot revolution" that could reshape global manufacturing, emphasizing the need for China to strengthen its robotics capabilities and compete for a larger share of the market. During the Long March, the Red Army fought the enemy with outdated weapons. Today, the challenge is different: keeping pace with the scientific revolution and the explosion of technological innovation. As the pressure of overseas technology restrictions and trade barriers rises, Xi directs the country to strengthen independent innovation and the resilience of industrial and supply chains, and ensure both development and security. He spearheaded a campaign to build China into a sci-tech powerhouse, elevating the country to the world's forefront in fields such as artificial intelligence, quantum technology and new energy. From carrier rockets to nuclear submarines, China has named some of its major technological achievements after the Long March, honoring a history of self-reliance and perseverance while inspiring new technological advances. In 2014, Xi led high-ranking generals to Gutian in Fujian, where a 1929 Red Army meeting established the principle of the Party's absolute leadership over the army, to reinforce that principle. He initiated a sweeping military reform, laying the groundwork for achieving the goals for the centenary of the People's Liberation Army in 2027 and building world-class armed forces. The new Long March is progressing steadily with significant results. From 2012 to 2025, China's GDP grew from about 54 trillion yuan to more than 140 trillion yuan, while per capita GDP rose from just over 6,000 to nearly 14,000 U.S. dollars. The country has built a complete industrial system covering all industrial categories in the United Nations classification. China's economy remains the largest engine of global growth, accounting for roughly one-third of the increase in global output in recent years, according to data from the Chinese government and international institutes. China's technology and cultural influence are also increasingly viewed positively around the world. A global survey released by the Pew Research Center in July found that views of China had improved in many countries in recent years. For the first time, China was viewed more favorably than the United States in a majority of the countries surveyed. Yet, as the 2035 modernization target draws closer, Xi has warned against complacency. "There are still many 'snowy mountains' and 'grasslands' for us to cross," Xi said. Meeting those challenges hinges above all on strengthening the Party's leadership. The historical parallel is explicit. The Long March helped form a new central leadership with Mao at its core and opened a period in which the Party increasingly found its own answers to the problems the Chinese revolution faced. "After the Long March, the Party and the Red Army were stronger, not weaker," Xi said. "This is because they had found the right path and the theory to guide them." In the new era, the Party established Xi's core position on the Party Central Committee and in the Party as a whole and established the guiding role of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Lu Yi, a professor at the Party School of the CPC Central Committee, said navigating the challenges of the new Long March requires sound strategic direction from the Party's leadership, unity within the CPC and across the country, as well as discipline, commitment and dedication among all Party members. "This is how the steel was tempered," said Yuri Tavrovsky, a Russian expert on China. "The dramatic events of 1934-1936 brought to the fore and strengthened the CPC's finest qualities, enabling it to unite a divided country and build a great one." ALL FOR THE PEOPLE In his masterpiece "Red Star Over China," first published in 1937, Snow recorded a Red Army soldier's simple explanation of what he and his comrades were fighting for: "Here everybody fights to help the poor, and to save China." Lu, the Party school professor, said that the history of the Red Army's epic march is also a history of the deep bonds between the army and the people, and of how the Party relied on the very people it sought to serve. In Yudu, residents took down doors and dismantled beds to build makeshift bridges that carried the Red Army across the river. Along the Long March, local people supplied them with food, served as guides and sheltered the wounded. "Back then, we relied on the people at every turn. We relied on them for food, and to fight our battles we had to mobilize them and rely on their support. Without them, we could not have accomplished anything," said Xi's father, Xi Zhongxun, when recalling his early revolutionary years. That reliance on the people remains central to Xi's approach to governance. He has stressed that the Party must work for the people and draw on their wisdom and initiative, grounding its policies in their needs and experience. Xi called on officials to draw inspiration from the Long March spirit and better understand the Party's original mission, which is "to seek happiness for the Chinese people and rejuvenation for the Chinese nation." He once recounted the story of "half a quilt." During the Long March, three Red Army soldiers slept at a villager's home, where the family lacked adequate bedding. Before leaving, they cut their only quilt in half and gave one half to the family to help them keep warm. When Xi took the top office, the Party had been in power for more than six decades, and some of its members had increasingly strayed from the traditions forged during the revolutionary years. Xi condemned some officials for being so brazen in their misconduct, including cronyism, factionalism, dangling official posts and feigned compliance -- practices that alienated the Party from the people. Xi warned that unchecked corruption could spell the end of both the Party and the state. He soon introduced a code of conduct known as the eight-point rules to curb official extravagance. He launched the largest anti-corruption drive in the Party's history, which has seen millions of people investigated for disciplinary violations. He also led improvements to the internal Party regulatory framework and established supervision commissions, all to "confine power to an institutional cage." Earlier this year, Xi initiated a Party-wide study campaign, prodding Party members to fix their mindset regarding governance performance. A key target is to stamp out the tendency among some officials to sacrifice public well-being in seeking to polish their performance records. "Ultimately, the Long March succeeded because the Party and the Red Army stood together with the people, maintained a close bond with the people, and shared weal and woe with the people. This is also a fundamental guarantee that enables us to overcome all difficulties and dangers," Xi said. Sustaining that bond means understanding what people hope for and acting on their most urgent concerns. Xi spearheaded an unprecedented poverty alleviation campaign that lifted nearly 100 million rural residents out of absolute poverty over eight years. Since the start of reform and opening up in 1978, over 70 percent of the world's poverty reduction has been attributed to China. Xi used Long March metaphors for the tough battle against poverty. "Just as Liupan Mountain was the last high peak the Red Army had to cross during the Long March, lifting all people out of poverty is the final summit we must overcome to build a moderately prosperous society in all respects," he said. Xi's anti-poverty war was vast in scale but granular in its approach, reaching into individual households to identify what kept them poor. Aid was tailored accordingly -- fostering industries suited to local conditions and relocating villagers out of inhospitable places. Over eight years, more than 3 million cadres were sent to villages to work on the frontline of fighting extreme poverty. As in the Long March, some never lived to see the victory: more than 1,800 Party members and officials died in the line of duty. Xi has described the willingness to make sacrifices for the country and its people, whatever the hardship, as central to the spirit of the Long March. An aerial drone photo taken on July 3, 2025 shows a solar power station for agricultural use in Weining County, southwest China's Guizhou Province. (Xinhua/Tao Liang) The snow-capped mountains and grasslands that the Red Army had to surmount on foot are now linked by highways and railways. China has built the world's largest expressway and high-speed railway networks, which have brought agricultural products out of remote villages to boost income for local residents. Ecological restoration is another feat. China has become the country with the largest and fastest increase in forest area worldwide. At the foot of the mountains along the Long March routes, ordinary visitors today may encounter giant pandas and other wild animals. Photovoltaic and wind power installations rise from the grasslands. Kerosene lamps that herders once provided to the Red Army are now mostly seen in museums. The country has also built the world's largest education, social security and health-care systems. Life expectancy reached 79.25 years in 2025. China now ranks among the best in upper-middle-income countries on major health indicators. The Long March China pursues today requires no less effort than the historic Long March, British scholar Martin Jacques said. "It's a complicated challenge, but there's so much possibility and so much potential in that. And the rewards will be enormous," he said. ECHO ACROSS THE WORLD The international community, according to Xi, increasingly believes that the Long March was one of the key events that shaped world history in the 20th century, regarding it as an epic of ideals, devotion, willpower, and bravery whose inspirational power has transcended time and borders. In the 1930s, Snow anticipated that someone would one day write the full epic of the Long March. In the decades since, many people have retraced its path, sought out survivors and written their own accounts. Among the best-known was American journalist Harrison Salisbury, who in his 1985 book "The Long March: The Untold Story" described the Long March as "sui generis," with its heroism firing the dreams of a huge nation and setting it moving toward a destiny no man can yet divine. Kenyan military officer Felix Gitaari Njage, among more than 100 officers from over 80 countries and regions who were studying in China, visited sites along the Long March routes this summer. He said the Long March spirit is a precious asset for the world, offering lessons for military personnel across nations. "Its underlying spirit offers countries of the Global South strategic wisdom and intellectual strength for achieving unity and self-reliance and overcoming adversity," he said. This photo taken on April 10, 2026 shows part of a programmable quantum computing prototype called "Jiuzhang 4.0." (Xinhua/Zhou Mu) The Long March continues to draw interest from scholars in both developed and developing countries. They believe China's success in the new Long March would benefit people beyond its borders as well as its own population. In 2013, Xi put forward the vision of a "community with a shared future for humanity." The vision, together with the initiatives he later proposed on global development, security, civilization and governance, set out China's proposals and solutions to tackle shared challenges in a world marked by wealth gaps, conflicts, mistrust, unilateralism and bullying. In September, at the BRICS summit in India, Xi urged the grouping to take the lead in promoting innovation, peace and stability, exchanges between civilizations, and reform of global governance. Kirill Babaev, director of the Institute of China and Modern Asia at the Russian Academy of Sciences, interpreted China's message as a call for other major countries to join a "new Long March" toward an international order based on equality and mutual respect. Its outcome, in his assessment, would matter to all humanity, not only to China. Keith Bennett, vice chairman of Britain's 48 Group, has drawn a similar connection between revolutionary memory and international cooperation. Writing in "China Today" in July, he said that the spirit of the Long March now finds expression in projects such as the Belt and Road Initiative, which connects countries through infrastructure, trade and development. The Long March, he wrote, remains a guiding force in tackling difficult and complex tasks, overcoming development bottlenecks, and pressing ahead with long-term national goals. For countries that look to China's experience, its efforts to combine development with security, shift toward cleaner energy, and advocate common prosperity may offer insights into addressing challenges such as climate change, public health emergencies, food and energy insecurity, and inequality. The Long March stands as a powerful testament to the boundless strength of the human spirit once awakened, said Professor Lu. "It offers confidence to developing countries and hope to all humanity, affirming that even in a world rife with uncertainties, there are still forces steadfastly defending justice and striving toward a brighter future," he said. The horizon stretches far ahead. The first of China's "two centenary goals" has been achieved. The second, tied to the People's Republic's centenary in 2049, still lies ahead. "Today, we are closer, more confident, and more capable than ever of reaching the goal of rejuvenating the Chinese nation," Xi said. "We will strive to safeguard world peace and development as we pursue our own development," he added. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: China edges U.S. for first women's team world gymnastics title in 20 years
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
China edges U.S. for first women's team world gymnastics title in 20 years Gold medalists team China (C), silver medalists team USA and bronze medalists team Japan celebrate during the awarding ceremony for the women's team final at Artistic Gymnastics World Championships 2026 in Rotterdam, the Netherlands, Oct. 21, 2026. (Xinhua/Weng Xinyang) ROTTERDAM, the Netherlands, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- China edged the United States by 0.233 points to claim its first women's team title in 20 years at the World Artistic Gymnastics Championships here on Wednesday. China topped the standings with 165.764 points, ahead of the United States with 165.531 and Japan with 164.063. The victory gave China its second women's world team title after its breakthrough triumph in 2006 and ended the United States' run of seven consecutive titles. All three medal-winning teams secured qualification for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games. China, which led qualification, turned the contest around on balance beam after trailing the United States through the opening two rotations. The United States posted the highest team totals on vault and uneven bars, scoring 42.633 and 42.766 respectively, while China recorded 40.966 and 42.466 on the same apparatus. Those scores left China 1.967 points behind at the halfway stage. The balance beam changed the complexion of the contest. Zhang Qingying delivered 15.066 points, the highest beam score of the final, while Ke Qinqin contributed 14.400 and Qiu Qiyuan added 13.900. China's combined 43.366, compared with the United States' 39.199, turned the deficit into a 2.200-point advantage heading into the final rotation. The United States fought back on floor exercise, where Claire Pease scored 13.933, Dulcy Caylor 13.600 and Reese Esponda 13.400 for a team total of 40.933. China responded with 13.033 from Zhang and 13.100 from Ke before Qiu closed the competition with 12.833, enough to preserve a narrow winning margin. Japan's bronze ended a 60-year wait for a women's team medal at the World Championships, with its previous podium finish coming in 1966. Aiko Sugihara contributed 14.200 on vault and 13.900 on floor to help Japan finish comfortably ahead of fourth-placed France. France scored 161.130, followed by Brazil with 159.730, Russia with 159.394, Italy with 158.129 and Canada with 158.096. The championships continue with the men's all-around final on Thursday and the women's all-around final on Friday, followed by the apparatus finals over the weekend. item.title: Cargo throughput of Pinglu Canal surpasses 1 mln tonnes in S China's Guangxi
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
Cargo throughput of Pinglu Canal surpasses 1 mln tonnes in S China's Guangxi An aerial drone photo taken on Oct. 21, 2026 shows cargo vessels passing through the Madao hub on the Pinglu Canal in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. Cargo throughput of the Pinglu Canal has surpassed 1 million tonnes since its opening to navigation on Sept. 16. The 134.2-kilometer canal runs from Nanning, capital of south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, to the Beibu Gulf, the closest maritime outlet for much of southwest China. The canal stretches along the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, a strategic trade route connecting China's inland regions with ASEAN and other global markets. It is the first river-to-sea canal project planned and coordinated at the national level since the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949. item.title: Grassland city in N China's Inner Mongolia transforms into an AI computing hub
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
Grassland city in N China's Inner Mongolia transforms into an AI computing hub Swans glide across the waters of Chahannur National Wetland Park in Shangdu county, Ulanqab, north China's Inner Mongolia autonomous region, on March 19, 2026. (People's Daily Online/Wang Zheng) How long does it take to travel from Ulanqab in north China's Inner Mongolia autonomous region to Beijing? By high-speed rail, roughly 100 minutes. Yet data traverses the same distance -- more than 240 kilometers -- in just 2.1 milliseconds via high-capacity fiber-optic cables. Harnessing its abundant wind resources and cool climate, Ulanqab is rapidly emerging as a major computing hub. As of the end of August, the city had secured agreements for 109 computing projects, covering more than 7 million standard server racks, with 190,000 petaflops of computing capacity already in operation. A Goldman Sachs report says that Ulanqab has emerged as one of the largest and fastest-growing AI computing clusters in the Asia-Pacific region. How did a once-isolated city with limited industrial diversification become a rising force on the national and global stage? For generations, Ulanqab's harsh winters, low rainfall, and brief growing season constrained traditional agriculture. Its economy has long depended on farming and livestock, leaving many communities vulnerable to climatic fluctuations. The city was once a key target of China's poverty alleviation campaign. Over the decades, Ulanqab has earned a string of nicknames, including China's "potato capital," "oat capital," and "wind power capital," each reflecting its distinctive geography and economy. Times have changed. Driven by the "East Data, West Computing" initiative, Ulanqab, this once austere landscape, is breaking free from the constraints of its traditional development path, rapidly emerging as a hub for cloud computing, AI computing, and token production. Behind this transformation lies a reimagining of how its natural resources can drive development. Computing infrastructure requires enormous physical facilities. Servers run around the clock, creating two major challenges: securing a reliable power supply and dissipating the heat they generate. This gives the computing industry different location priorities from traditional manufacturing. It does not necessarily need to be near densely populated cities; instead, it places greater emphasis on energy costs, climate, and available land. In this new equation, Ulanqab's traditional geographic disadvantages are becoming assets in the digital age. Take wind energy first. Ulanqab experiences 60 days of strong winds in spring alone. Combined with an annual solar radiation of 5,500-6,200 megajoules per square meter, these conditions give the city abundant wind and solar resources. Its wind and solar farms rank among the nation's leaders in annual utilization hours, and installed renewable energy capacity has reached 20.67 million kilowatts. Computing is an electricity-intensive industry. The more servers a data center operates and the greater its computing capacity, the more power it needs. Ulanqab's wind and solar resources, once of limited use to traditional industries, now align with the massive electricity demand of data centers. Photo shows wind turbines at the wind and solar power facility operated by China Three Gorges Renewables (Group) Co., Ltd. in Siziwang Banner, Ulanqab, north China's Inner Mongolia autonomous region, on May 8, 2026. (People's Daily Online/Wang Zheng) Cold weather carries new meaning here too. For traditional agriculture and livestock farming, low average temperatures and a short frost-free season limit the growing season. For data centers, however, the same cold climate offers a natural source of cooling. Ulanqab's average summer temperature is just 18.8 degrees Celsius, and the region enjoys nearly 10 months of natural cooling each year. Large data centers can use cool outdoor air to dissipate heat, reducing energy consumption by an estimated 30 percent. What once constrained agricultural production has become an economic resource that directly lowers computing costs. Then there's proximity. "Just a 'step' west of Beijing lies Ulanqab" is a slogan that captures the city's close proximity to the capital. Ulanqab is over 300 kilometers from Beijing. For traditional goods, that distance can mean lengthy transport times and high logistics costs. For data, however, a dedicated 144-fiber, dual-route link to Beijing enables ultra-low-latency transmission. Powered by green electricity, natural cooling and ultra-low-latency connectivity, Ulanqab is meeting growing demand from the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region for AI training, autonomous driving R&D and big data processing. By converting its natural and geographic advantages into digital hub strengths, the city is emerging as a green computing powerhouse. Leading companies in AI and smart vehicles are setting up operations there, driving the development of a full industrial chain spanning computing infrastructure, hardware manufacturing, cybersecurity, data services and talent training. Ulanqab is emerging as a key hub in China's integrated national computing network. Ulanqab is evolving from a transportation hub into a computing hub, unlocking new avenues for growth in the digital economy. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Xi calls for new achievements on new Long March
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
Xi calls for new achievements on new Long March Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, delivers an important speech during a gathering commemorating the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Red Army's Long March held at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 22, 2026. (Xinhua/Xie Huanchi) BEIJING, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday called for new achievements on the new Long March as China commemorates the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Red Army's Long March. "Only by remembering history can we create a brighter future," said Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, when addressing a gathering held in Beijing to mark the anniversary. Under Xi's proposal, all participants stood up and observed a moment of silence for the revolutionary heroes who gave their lives during the Long March and in revolutionary struggles across China. From October 1934 to October 1936, the Red Army marched through more than 10 provinces during the Long March, opening up a new chapter in the Chinese revolution, Xi said. "This earth-shattering revolutionary feat holds great significance in the history of our Party, country and military, and has a profound impact on our path toward the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation," he noted. Xi stressed that the Party's right leadership and the establishment of Mao Zedong's core position were decisive for the victory of the Red Army's Long March. The Party and the Red Army relied on firm conviction, Xi said, adding that troops with noble ideals and firm beliefs are invincible. Xi emphasized the importance of integrating the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities in addressing the country's issues and problems. He further underscored that the people will always be the source of strength and a strong support for the Party and the people's armed forces. A gathering commemorating the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Red Army's Long March is held at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 22, 2026. (Xinhua/Ding Haitao) Xi said the great spirit of the Long March demonstrates the power of loyalty, truth, justice and unity. "It will always be a precious treasure and a powerful driving force inspiring us to overcome difficulties and forge ahead courageously." He said the road of the Long March continues to extend. "On our new journey, we are now committed to realizing the Second Centenary Goal of building China into a great modern socialist country in all respects and advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation on all fronts through a Chinese path to modernization," he said. To forge ahead on the new Long March, Xi said, it is imperative to stay committed to the Party's ideals, convictions and purpose and rely closely on the people to create new achievements. He underscored the need to unswervingly advance high-quality development and promote common prosperity for all. Efforts must be made to better ensure both development and security and seize the historical initiative to overcome difficulties, combat risks and meet challenges, he stressed. Xi also emphasized the importance of moving more quickly to reinforce the people's armed forces to world-class standards and adhering to the Party's absolute leadership over the military. It is also vital to uphold the leadership of the Party, strengthen Party building and persevere with full and rigorous Party self-governance, he added. Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang and Li Xi, who are members of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, as well as Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, attended the gathering. A gathering commemorating the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Red Army's Long March is held at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 22, 2026. Xi Jinping, Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang, Li Xi and Han Zheng attended the gathering. (Xinhua/Xie Huanchi) Zhao, who presided over the event, said Xi's speech was of immense political, ideological and guiding significance, urging earnest efforts to study and grasp its essence and ensure its effective implementation. He called on the whole Party, the entire military and the Chinese people of all ethnic groups to rally more closely around the Party Central Committee with Xi at its core and strive to build a great country and advance national rejuvenation on all fronts through Chinese modernization. Around 3,000 people participated in the gathering at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.
